title: Dzogchen
hookLine: the "great perfection" of the Nyingma school: awareness already complete

cards: A mirror hangs in a hallway. All day, things pass in front of it: a child with a muddy face, a bouquet of flowers, someone crying, someone laughing, a dog.
The mirror shows every one of them completely, and when each walks away, it's exactly as it was. The mud didn't dirty it. The flowers didn't make it more beautiful.
Nobody had to polish it into being a mirror. It already was one. The Nyingma school of Tibet points at the mind with a picture like this.

teach.b: First, the name. Dzogchen is Tibetan, usually translated the great perfection, or the great completeness.
In Nyingma teaching, which you met earlier this year, it's the summit of the whole path, the last of their nine vehicles. Second, the claim, which is bold.

Nyingma teachers say the mind's basic awareness, which they call rigpa, is already complete. Practice doesn't manufacture it. Like the mirror, it shows everything, is stained by nothing, and needs nothing added.
What we usually call the mind, the running commentary, the worries, the plans, is like the things passing in front of the glass.
Third, the three statements. Tradition credits a teacher named Garab Dorje with summing up Dzogchen in three short lines, which the Nyingma master Patrul Rinpoche later explained in a commentary.
In plain words: be introduced directly to your own nature. Decide on this one thing, without doubt. Gain confidence that thoughts free themselves as they arise.
That last one is the surprise. A thought doesn't have to be fought or fixed. Seen for what it is, it dissolves on its own, like writing on water.
Fourth, what that does not mean.

Not doing nothing, or drifting, or giving up on kindness. Nyingma teachers say ethics, compassion and the preliminary practices still matter, and that resting in rigpa is very different from spacing out.
The ease is the fruit of long preparation.
But the starting point is turned around: what's being looked for is already here. Stop covering it up.

how: In the Nyingma school, Dzogchen is taught as the summit of the path: after preliminary practices, a teacher introduces the student to rigpa, the mind's basic awareness, and the student trains in resting in it and letting thoughts free themselves.

o: a Tibetan word for a polished temple mirror
a strict program of perfect conduct, rule by rule
the great perfection: awareness already complete

games.q: the great perfection: tap the pairs.

s: in Dzogchen, awareness has to be built up by long effort
Nyingma teachers say rigpa is already complete; practice stops covering it up.
resting in rigpa is the same as spacing out
teachers say it is very different from drifting, and comes after long preparation.
the third statement says thoughts free themselves as they arise
seen for what it is, a thought dissolves on its own, like writing on water.

games.q: you're resting in practice and notice an angry thought. what does Dzogchen teaching say to do with it?
o: see it for what it is and let it free itself.
follow it to find out who's to blame.
games.why: in the third statement, thoughts free themselves as they arise when seen for what they are, like writing on water.

practice: Sit with your eyes open and your gaze wide and soft, taking in the whole room without landing anywhere.
Whatever shows up, a sound, an itch, a thought about dinner, let it show up the way things show up in a mirror, and don't improve your posture, your breath or your mind.
If you catch yourself fixing, notice that too, and rest as the mirror.

wordCard.voice: Dzogchen. The great perfection of the Nyingma school: the teaching that awareness, rigpa, is already complete, like a mirror nothing can stain. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit atiyoga, a name used for Dzogchen as the last of the Nyingma's nine vehicles.

carryVoice: Your line: already complete. Like the mirror, never dirtied by what passes in front of it. Back tomorrow, same hill.
